title: Cohomology properties of maps in (Cat) : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting, from the previous page: a basic (fundamental) localizer W on (Cat). X' is a small category with a 'closed' full subcategory Y' and open complement U'. Here Y' is a cosieve: arrows u'→y' may exist, none go back. f: X→X' is a cofibration (Grothendieck opfibration) with Y = f^{-1}(Y'), U = f^{-1}(U') and U→U' an isomorphism. g = f|Y : Y→Y' and i: Y→X is the inclusion.

Page (1) showed that under the cofibration hypothesis the square (i, g; f, i') is cocartesian in Cat, i.e. X' = X ⊔_Y Y'. It also described such data as a functor Φ: Y'→Cat plus a bifunctor Hom(u',y')→Ob Φ(y'): a gluing ('recollement') description.

This page asks for the strict pushout to also be a homotopy pushout. Let ∫(i,g) be the Grothendieck construction of the span X ←i– Y –g→ Y', fibered over the category a←c→b. It is the standard model of the homotopy pushout (Thomason). The wish is that the canonical comparison ∫(i,g) → lim→(span) = X ⊔_Y Y' = X' lies in W, and better, that it is W-aspherical (all comma categories ∫(i,g)/x' are W-aspherical).

Strategy 1. The hypotheses are stable under every base change X'_1 → X' (drawn as a cube). If the square ∫(i_1,g_1) → ∫(i,g) over X'_1 → X' is cartesian ('à vérifier'), the map would be universally in W. It is in fact cartesian: objects and morphisms of ∫ are computed componentwise over X'.

Strategy 2, more direct. ∫(i,g) → X' is itself a cofibration, and its fibers are W-aspherical:
- Over x' ∈ U' the fiber is a point e, since X_{x'} ≅ e and nothing from Y or Y' lies over x'.
- Over y' ∈ Y' the fiber is the Grothendieck construction of Y_{y'} ←id– Y_{y'} → e. This is weakly equivalent to the cone C(Y_{y'}), which has a final object, hence is aspherical.

For a cofibration p: E→B, each fiber inclusion E_b → E/b has a left adjoint (cocartesian pushforward), so it lies in W. Hence a cofibration with aspherical fibers is aspherical, and this persists under any base change: the map is universally W-aspherical, in particular in W.

Page '2 bis' then states this as a theorem: cofibration plus disjointness of fibers implies the square is homotopy cocartesian. It corrects the fiber description to C(A) ⊔_A (A×Δ^1), a deformation retract onto the cone. It draws the corollaries i∈W ⇒ i'∈W and g∈W ⇒ f∈W.

Purpose: an excision / Mayer–Vietoris type statement in Cat for an arbitrary basic localizer. Strict pushouts along closed (cosieve) inclusions with an opfibration condition are homotopy pushouts. This is the kind of property needed for comparing Cat with homotopy types and for 'cohomological properties of maps in Cat'.
errors: The fiber over y' ∈ Y' is not the cone C(Y_{y'}) itself and has no final object. It is ∫(Y_{y'} ← Y_{y'} → e) ≅ C(A) ⊔_A (A×Δ^1). It is only weakly equivalent to (a deformation retract onto) the cone, which has a final object. Grothendieck corrects this on the next page; the conclusion (fiber W-aspherical) stands.
Notational slip: 'x ∈ X \ Y'' should read x' ∈ X' \ Y' = U'.

The cartesianness of the base-change square is left as 'à vérifier'. It is true (∫ is computed fiberwise over X'), but the argument is anyway superseded by the cofibration-with-aspherical-fibers argument, which is stable under base change.

ideas.what: Grothendieck construction of a span as model of the homotopy pushout; comparison map to the strict pushout
ideas.modern_name: Thomason's homotopy colimit theorem (hocolim = Grothendieck construction)
ideas.where_published: Les Dérivateurs / Pursuing Stacks use ∫ of diagrams of categories as homotopy colimits (general idea; exact form unsure)

ideas.what: A cofibration (opfibration) with W-aspherical fibers is W-aspherical, universally under base change
ideas.modern_name: Quillen Theorem A style criterion for Grothendieck opfibrations relative to a basic localizer
ideas.usually_credited_to: Quillen 1973; Grothendieck (Pursuing Stacks); Maltsiniotis, Cisinski for basic localizers
ideas.where_published: Pursuing Stacks (asphericity, fibrations/cofibrations); systematized in Maltsiniotis, Astérisque 301

ideas.what: Strict pushout along a closed (cosieve) inclusion, where the comparison functor is an opfibration iso over the open complement, is a homotopy pushout for any basic localizer; corollaries i∈W⇒i'∈W, g∈W⇒f∈W
ideas.modern_name: Homotopy cocartesianness of pushouts along sieves/Dwyer maps in Cat
ideas.usually_credited_to: Thomason 1980 (Dwyer maps, Thomason model structure); Cisinski (Astérisque 308 / 'Le localisateur fondamental minimal') for general fundamental localizers
ideas.where_published: Not known in circulated texts; this page and the archive cote 118

ideas.what: Description of opfibrations over X' trivial over the open U' by a functor Φ: Y'→Cat plus a bifunctor Hom(u',y')→Ob Φ(y')
ideas.modern_name: Artin gluing / recollement of opfibrations along an open–closed decomposition
ideas.where_published: SGA4 for toposes; not for Cat in this form

missed.claim: Grothendieck proves, via 'cofibration with aspherical fibers', that the strict pushout along a closed subcategory, with the comparison functor an opfibration iso off the closed part, is universally a homotopy pushout for any basic localizer W. Analogous results in the literature are credited to Thomason (Dwyer maps) and later Cisinski. This independent opfibration-based variant from ~1983 is not recorded as Grothendieck's, though the result itself is essentially known.
missed.quote: Mais on vérifie directement que ∫(i,g) → X' est cofibré à fibres W-asphériques
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical credit; the hypothesis (opfibration rather than Dwyer map) gives a clean, base-change-stable criterion, but comparable statements exist.

deep.surprise_reason: Careful, correct working of a homotopy-pushout/excision statement in Cat for basic localizers. The method and result are close to known work of Thomason and Cisinski/Maltsiniotis; mainly of historical interest.

Last lines read roughly: '≃ C(Y_{y'}) pour x' = y' ∈ Y'', with the cone annotated as having a final point ('à point final'); 'Y_y!' refers to the fiber Y_{y'}.
